video_title: Will Struggling Nvidia Take The Markets Down With It? | Lance Roberts
gist: Lance Roberts and Adam Taggart dissect Jensen Huang's scandal-driven exit from NVIDIA as a key-man risk event, arguing the stock (10 forward P/E, 0.12 PEG, ~4 std devs oversold) is fundamentally cheap but should be bought in tranches after next week's earnings and congressional hearings, with $120 as the heavy-buy level. They also see last Thursday's plunge as a one-day hedge-fund liquidation, a contrarian year-end rally setup backed by buybacks and seasonality, limited federal impact from the midterm blue wave, and AI capex slowdown as the key macro risk.

themes.theme: Jensen Huang ouster and NVIDIA key-man risk

insights.claim: Jensen Huang has resigned as NVIDIA CEO after an alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy and further affairs with NVIDIA executives, and has been replaced by the CFO, with an additional board seat added for more controls.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Leadership vacuum at the market's most important stock is a fresh idiosyncratic risk for index-heavy portfolios.
insights.quote: he has resigned and he has been replaced by the CFO.

insights.claim: NVIDIA had no succession plan: Huang ran a flat organization as chairman, CEO, public face and chief lobbyist while maintaining complete control.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Absence of a successor amplifies disruption and lengthens the period of uncertainty for the stock.
insights.quote: There was no succession plan. He ran a very flat organization and he maintained maintained complete control.

insights.claim: Key-man risk is pervasive across the AI leaders — OpenAI (Sam Altman), Anthropic (Dario), and Elon Musk's companies — leaving the tip of the AI spear unusually vulnerable to the loss of single individuals.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Price key-person risk into concentrated AI exposure; single-person events can move entire sectors.

insights.claim: China's goal with the alleged spy may not have been stealing secrets but engineering a scandal that removes NVIDIA's key leader to slow America's AI effort.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Geopolitical interference is a new, unpriced risk factor for the AI megatrend.

insights.claim: Historically, stocks of companies that ousted CEOs for conduct reasons averaged roughly an 11% loss over the following year, with Coles (spelled as in captions) in 2025 as a notable exception that did well.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Base rate argues for a tough year for NVIDIA even if the selloff looks overdone.

insights.claim: Across 17 conduct-driven CEO removals, stocks were trading about 4.7% higher within 12 months on average, but with a worst point of -32% during the period, so outcomes depend heavily on the starting point (Lance cited conflicting averages of -11%, ~1% and +4.7% in the discussion).
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Wide dispersion after conduct ousters means size positions small and use stops rather than bet on the average.

insights.claim: Huang's removal does not change NVIDIA's earnings power because engineers, employees, sales and customers remain in place; the company loses its face, not its production.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: If fundamentals are intact, scandal-driven weakness can become a long-term buying opportunity.
insights.quote: Jensen Huang isn't building the chips. He's not building the GPUs. The engineers are still working.

insights.claim: There is a small possibility Jensen Huang returns as NVIDIA CEO if congressional investigations find no national security breach, given strong ecosystem support; otherwise Elon Musk said he would hire him 'in a heartbeat.'
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A reinstatement headline would be a sharp upside catalyst for NVIDIA.

insights.claim: CEO track records matter little to boards because companies keep recycling executives from the same CEO pool, as when Home Depot hired a CEO who had already bankrupted another company.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Don't assume a disgraced or failed executive is gone; expect Huang to resurface as a CEO somewhere.

insights.claim: A possible divorce could lead Huang's wife to sell a large NVIDIA stake (estimated at $60-80 billion), adding another source of downward pressure on the stock.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Watch for any forced/elective insider liquidation as overhang on NVIDIA supply.

insights.claim: NVIDIA trades at a 0.12 PEG ratio and about a 10 forward P/E, almost four standard deviations below its moving average, making it fundamentally cheap and deeply oversold; even pre-scandal its P/E was said to be below Coca-Cola's.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Extreme value/oversold readings set up a tradable bounce in NVIDIA.
insights.quote: It trades at a 0.12 PEG ratio and a 10 forward PE. I mean, if I can buy NVIDIA at a 10 forward PE, it's pretty cheap

insights.claim: Any NVIDIA bounce will meet trapped sellers, so the stock likely retests lows or sets higher lows while grinding through a 6-10 month repair process.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Trade bounces, but don't expect a V-shaped recovery; build positions slowly.
insights.quote: It's a tradable bounce. You can certainly make some money in it, but it's going to probably eventually either retest lows or set higher lows

insights.claim: On the monthly chart NVIDIA is around $160 with downside to roughly $120 at its four-year moving average, a level it has corrected to and held twice before, where Lance would be a heavy buyer.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: $120 is the key long-term accumulation level to watch; ~25% downside remains possible.
insights.quote: This stock could travel down to 120 and I'd be a heavy buyer around 120

insights.claim: NVIDIA reports earnings Tuesday followed by congressional hearings Wednesday; investors with no exposure should wait through both events before buying, or start only a small position with a tight stop (buy ~160, stop ~155).
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Event risk next week; use earnings and hearings as the gate for entering tranches.
insights.quote: If you've got no exposure, just wait through earnings and wait through the congressional hearings next week.

insights.claim: RIA's NVIDIA process is three tranches: buy one when a bottom forms, add a second on buy signals, and a third as recovery proceeds, always with stop losses rather than falling into the 'hope cycle.'
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A disciplined scaling-in template for buying beaten-down leaders.

insights.claim: RIA still owns NVIDIA with no principal left at risk after repeated profit-taking, holds it below market weight, and plans to return it to target weight and then overweight once it bottoms because it is fundamentally cheap.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A long-time holder plans to add, not sell — a signal of fundamental conviction.

insights.claim: NVIDIA is trading back where it was around February of this year, so the decline should be kept in perspective.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Year-to-date context tempers panic about the drawdown.

themes.theme: Market technicals, liquidations and year-end setup

insights.claim: The S&P broke its consolidation channel and hit the 200-day moving average at about 7,366 as predicted, bounced, then was rejected at the 50-day moving average, and is now back where it was in May.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: 200-DMA (~7,366) is support and the 50/20-DMA is resistance; a break above signals trend resumption.

insights.claim: A rally early next week would trigger a momentum buy signal from a fairly low level, and with markets oversold and sentiment very bearish, this is a strong contrarian setup for a short-term rally.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Bearish consensus plus oversold breadth favors a near-term upside trade.
insights.quote: This is a really good contrarian setup. Everybody's expecting the market to go down lower.

insights.claim: Last Thursday's top-five-biggest down day was essentially a one-day bloodletting driven by forced liquidation of several leveraged hedge funds, which is why markets rallied hard afterward; Lance is watching whether Leopold (Situational Awareness) was among the casualties.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Liquidation-driven flushes tend to be followed by recoveries rather than sustained declines.
insights.quote: it was pretty much a one-day blood letting. And there were several hedge funds that got basically liquidated.

insights.claim: Record margin debt and record hedge-fund leverage mean that modest underperformance can trigger rapid liquidations.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Elevated leverage raises tail risk of sudden air pockets; keep stops and cash.
insights.quote: margin debt, which is it's a double-edged sword and unfortunately, the edge that cuts you cuts the deepest.

insights.claim: Markets tend to perform fairly well after volatility spikes like last week's, once offside positioning is flushed out.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Post-spike periods historically favor buying rather than selling.

insights.claim: Year-end tailwinds for tech include hedge funds and pensions needing to re-gross heavily liquidated, underweight tech books, strong earnings, and an open buyback window with about $1.5 trillion in announced buybacks on track.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Flows favor a year-end rally led by beaten-down growth/tech.
insights.quote: We're on track for 1.5 trillion in announcements for buybacks.

insights.claim: Seasonally, November and December are decent, except the first two weeks of December when mutual funds sell for capital-gains distributions, typically creating a buying opportunity before the Santa Claus rally funded by redeployed cash.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Use early-December weakness to add ahead of the year-end rally.

insights.claim: RIA's fear/greed gauge and money flow breadth indicator are at extremely low levels, contrarian signals that markets are better positioned to rally than fall, though RIA is holding extra cash and using stops.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Contrarian sentiment indicators argue for leaning long with risk controls.

insights.claim: RIA's Michael is more nervous about 2027 than the next two months, while the firm's base case is a rally into year end.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Near-term bullish, longer-term caution — consider tightening risk heading into 2027.

themes.theme: Inflation, rates and the oil/consumer picture

insights.claim: The hot CPI print was not surprising because oil ran almost to $100 a barrel; consensus CPI estimates of 0.2% are useless because analysts just plug in the 25-year average of 2.4%/12.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Ignore consensus distributions; track oil as the real inflation driver.
insights.quote: 2.4% divided by 12 is 0.2. So they just plug in the average as their estimate

insights.claim: Rate-hike expectations rose after CPI, hitting rate-sensitive assets like precious metals and Bitcoin, but Lance expects much of that to reverse as weaker-than-expected PPI feeds into a weaker PCE print.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: A soft PCE could relieve rate-sensitive assets (gold, silver, Bitcoin, long-duration tech).
insights.quote: PPI came in on Friday weaker than expected. PCE is going to come in weaker than expected.

insights.claim: Higher rates weigh on long-duration assets via higher discount rates, which is why technology has been under pressure for the past three to four months.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Tech performance is tied to the rate path; falling hike odds would help.

insights.claim: Oil quietly fell to about $85 a barrel as Trump signaled he doesn't need an Iran deal and can rely on naval blockades, setting the table for not going kinetic, though prices could rise again.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Oil is a swing factor for inflation and consumer demand; watch Iran headlines.

insights.claim: Demand destruction from high fuel and food costs is visible in consumers, but AI data-center capex (adding about 0.4 percentage points to growth last quarter) is masking that weakness; ex-capex the economy would be much slower and disinflationary.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: The economy is dependent on AI capex; any slowdown there would expose consumer weakness.
insights.quote: CAPEX added about 4/10 of a percent to growth in the last quarter.

insights.claim: Housing affordability cannot be fixed by demand-side policies like down payment assistance, which raise demand and worsen the problem; only time under high rates (or more supply) restores affordability.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Expect affordability policies to be inflationary for housing rather than relieving.

themes.theme: Midterm blue wave and AI data-center politics

insights.claim: The midterm 'blue wave' brought candidates who oppose AI data-center buildout, and Lance alleges Chinese money flowed through NGOs into PACs to elect them so China could take the AI lead.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Policy risk to AI capex now has a geopolitical dimension; monitor state-level actions.

insights.claim: A federal data-center moratorium or tax-cut repeal is very low probability because Trump holds the veto; states can only pause new, not already-permitted, data centers, and Texas (about 25% of data centers) already had Greg Abbott impose a moratorium on new ones.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Near-term AI capex pipeline is largely protected; risk is to future projects.

insights.claim: Across 19 midterm elections, the S&P returned an average 15.1% over the next 12 months (15.5% with a Republican president and Democratic Congress), with no negative instances, and drawdowns like 1987 were short-lived.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Historical base rate strongly favors equities in the 12 months post-midterm.
insights.quote: 15.1% but when there's a a Republican president Democratic Congress it's 15.5.

insights.claim: Midterms don't set bond yields: over the last 19 midterms yields rose nine times and fell seven times with about a 4 basis point spread; economics and inflation drive yields.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Don't trade bonds on election outcomes; focus on inflation data.

insights.claim: Continuing resolutions add about 8% to the prior year's spending, so by the rule of 72 federal debt doubles about every nine years, and gridlock means more shutdowns and CRs that markets tend to shrug off.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Structural deficits persist regardless of party; shutdowns are typically buyable noise.
insights.quote: every nine years, the debt doubles because you're compounding at 8% a year.

insights.claim: If states like Ohio, Nevada and Texas pass moratoriums on new data centers, it would hurt the economy and the earnings of all companies, not just AI-related ones.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: State-level data-center restrictions are a key downside catalyst for broad earnings.

insights.claim: Adam's biggest market and economic concern is an unexpected slowdown in AI capex, which would force stock write-downs, reduce money entering the real economy and create a negative wealth effect; he sees the anti-data-center movement likely growing as voters focus on electricity costs and job fears.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: AI capex is the single biggest swing factor; monitor capex guidance and local opposition.

insights.claim: Presidential-cycle data show the third year is the best but every year is positive on average (third year up 36 times vs 12 down, fourth year 36 vs 11), so sitting in bonds outside year three would grossly underperform.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Don't time the cycle by exiting equities; stay invested.

insights.claim: Investors should tax-loss harvest beaten-down positions even in great companies like NVIDIA, sell and wait 31 days or swap into a correlated instrument such as a single-stock NVIDIA ETF, then use losses to rebalance big gainers to target weights.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Year-end harvesting cuts taxes and rebalances risk without abandoning exposure.
insights.quote: you could literally sell Nvidia and go buy a single stock Nvidia ETF. Because those are two different assets.

insights.claim: Physical precious metals are not SEC-regulated securities and reportedly are not subject to the wash-sale rule, so bullion can be sold and immediately rebought to capture losses (e.g., silver bought near $120 in January now below $50); swapping SLV for PSLV also preserves silver exposure — verify with a CPA.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Silver holders sitting on 50%+ losses can harvest them while keeping ounces.

insights.claim: RIA's factor rotation model is up about 29% for the year and its 60/40 model just hit a new high; the money flow and breadth indicator drove much of its earlier risk reduction and will be built into models.
insights.speaker: Lance Roberts
insights.so_what: Active factor rotation has outperformed this year; gauges are guiding RIA's positioning.
insights.quote: Our factor rotation model is our best performer. It's up like 29% for the year.
